title: Hexbin density: count overlapping points without hiding exposure
summary: Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.
body:
Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.

Overplotting is a counting problem

When thousands of marks overlap, a dark patch can reflect drawing order or opacity rather than a trustworthy count. Binning makes the count explicit. A hexagonal grid offers a compact neighborhood shape, but it still imposes a resolution and origin. Record both. Overplotting and sampling bias explain why a random sample may help inspection but cannot silently replace total-density reporting. Show how many points survived filtering and coordinate validation before any bins are painted.

Coordinate units determine the grid

A grid in longitude and latitude degrees does not represent equal ground area across latitudes. For a geographic density question, project coordinates into an appropriate metric system before choosing cell width. If this is only a relative screen-space view, say so and avoid claims about area-normalized risk. Keep projection, extent and grid origin fixed across time panels. Otherwise unchanged points may fall into different cells. Geographic rate maps have a related denominator problem.

Count and exposure answer different questions

A cell with 81 incidents may cover 810,000 journeys; a cell with 47 may cover 4,700. Count highlights workload, while incidents per journey describe a different quantity. Preserve zero-exposure cells separately from zero-incident cells. Dividing by drawn polygon area does not produce a population risk. The denominator contract must match the decision. If sparse cells are suppressed for privacy, label that suppression and retain a public aggregate total rather than pretending the hidden cells are zero.

Test resolution and edge effects

A coarse grid can merge two nearby clusters; a fine grid can fragment one. Inspect multiple declared widths while keeping the color domain comparable. Points exactly on the extent edge need a documented inclusion rule. Export each bin's identifier, center or polygon, count, exposure and suppression state so the chart can be checked without its pixels. The export manifest should retain projection, extent, width and origin. An accessible summary should identify the highest-count cells and explain the unit encoded by color.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import floor, isfinite

def audit_spatial_counts(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                         cell_width: float) -> Counter[tuple[int, int]]:
    if not isfinite(cell_width) or cell_width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("cell width must be positive")
    if any(not isfinite(x) or not isfinite(y) for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    return Counter((floor(x / cell_width), floor(y / cell_width))
                   for x, y in points)

depot_coordinates = [(47.2, 81.6), (47.7, 81.1), (59.4, 81.5)]
audit = audit_spatial_counts(depot_coordinates, 4)
assert audit[(11, 20)] == 2 and sum(audit.values()) == 3

Performance and operating cost

This rectangular audit grid takes O(N) expected time and O(B) space for N points and B occupied bins. It checks count conservation before passing projected coordinates to a hexbin renderer; rectangular cells and hexagons do not share identifiers. The renderer decides hexagon placement and edge rules. A real map also needs projection and exposure joins versioned with its bin table. Preserve input and retained counts to detect losses.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling raw incident counts a risk rate.
  • Using degree-based cells as if they had equal ground area.
  • Changing grid extent between periods and interpreting bin movement as behavior change.
  • Hiding suppressed or zero-exposure cells as ordinary zero counts.

Validation drill

Bin 810 projected service calls at two widths. Reconcile counts to input, attach journey exposure by cell and compare the busiest cell with the highest incident-rate cell.

title: Diverging bars: put signed differences on one shared zero
summary: Choose a meaningful reference, keep a shared scale and retain both values behind every gap.
body:
Choose a meaningful reference, keep a shared scale and retain both values behind every gap.

The reference is the argument

A diverging bar begins at zero and extends according to a signed difference. That zero must mean something: actual minus plan, current minus prior, or group A minus group B. Put the formula and unit near the axis. A negative result may mean a shortfall, a benefit or simply a lower measurement. Label the groups rather than assuming red always means bad. A shared baseline lets readers compare directions.

Keep both operands available

A difference of 34 could arise from 47 versus 81 or 4,700 versus 4,734. The same bar length does not reveal operational scale. Tooltips and exports should contain both values, the reference version and any denominator used to make a rate. If teams differ sharply in size, a rate difference may answer the comparison better than counts. Denominator design precedes color choice. A gap based on a missing or zero denominator is undefined, not a zero-length bar.

Sort for the decision

Ranking by signed difference groups shortfalls; ranking by absolute difference surfaces the largest departures in either direction. State the sort key. Do not reorder every small multiple independently if the reader must follow the same entity through time. Shared facet order preserves identity. For equal comparison of positive and negative magnitudes, set a symmetric numeric domain around zero. An asymmetric domain can compress one side. Never clip a long bar without an exact value label and visible break.

Expose uncertainty

A small bar near zero may be noise rather than stable movement. For estimates, add an interval marker and explain whether it crosses zero. The chart should not declare every positive value a success. A materiality threshold belongs on the plot only when its rule is documented and consistent across entities. Small-sample uncertainty matters most near the boundary. Include a text alternative listing signed gaps, both operands and the largest departures on either side.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def signed_plan_gaps(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float]]
                     ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("entity names must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(actual) or not isfinite(plan)
           for _, actual, plan in rows):
        raise ValueError("measurements must be finite")
    return sorted(((name, actual, plan, actual - plan)
                   for name, actual, plan in rows), key=lambda item: item[3])

depot_gaps = signed_plan_gaps([("north", 47, 81),
                              ("south", 113, 97),
                              ("west", 59, 59)])
assert depot_gaps[0] == ("north", 47, 81, -34)
assert depot_gaps[-1][3] == 16

Performance and operating cost

For N entities, computing differences takes O(N) time and sorting takes O(N log N) time with O(N) output space. Reusing order across facets avoids repeated sort decisions, though it may make one panel less locally ranked. The example calculates absolute signed differences. A rate gap needs validated denominators and a declared unit before plotting. A chart library's autoscale should not override a specified symmetric domain.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring negative bars as bad when lower is preferable.
  • Discarding the actual and plan values after calculating a gap.
  • Using unequal left and right scales to exaggerate one direction.
  • Confusing percentage-point change with percent change.

Validation drill

Plot 47 depots' actual-minus-plan gaps. Sort by signed difference, show both operands, then compare that ranking to a rate-gap view based on eligible volume.

title: Waterfall charts: reconcile every step to the closing total
summary: Model changes as signed contributions, and keep subtotals distinct from new contributions.
body:
Model changes as signed contributions, and keep subtotals distinct from new contributions.

A bridge is an equation

A waterfall begins with an opening amount, applies signed changes in a declared order, and ends with a closing amount. Every floating bar implies a cumulative level before and after its step. The diagram is useful when the question is why a total changed, but the numbers must reconcile exactly. An unexplained residual should be shown as a named residual, not hidden in the last bar. The aggregation grain must stay stable: summing transaction-level changes and mixing them with account-level balances can double count.

Separate a subtotal from a change

A subtotal displays the running balance at a checkpoint; it does not add to that balance again. A renderer may call an item relative, absolute or total, but the source data should declare its semantic role independently of the library. Recalculate every subtotal from the opening amount and preceding changes. If a reported checkpoint disagrees, stop the publication pipeline or show the discrepancy explicitly. The export contract should keep item role, signed amount, running level and source period.

Choose order without inventing causality

Steps may be ordered by business process, chronology or contribution magnitude. A magnitude order helps show large drivers but can imply a process order that never occurred; label it as a decomposition rather than an event timeline. If two drivers overlap, their estimated contributions may not be independently additive. State the allocation rule before drawing. Annotations and causal claims require more evidence than a visually convenient bridge. For an exact ledger, preserve source transaction IDs or reconciliation batches.

Read signed values and scale

A decrease may be good or bad depending on the metric. Use text and bar direction as well as color. A zero step should remain in the export but can be collapsed in a crowded display if the omission is stated. If the starting balance is negative, make zero visible and verify connectors still show the true running level. Signed comparison charts are better when the task is ranking independent gaps rather than explaining one total. Test refunds, reversals, missing steps and rounding before release.

Worked contract

from decimal import Decimal

def reconcile_bridge(opening: Decimal,
                     steps: list[tuple[str, Decimal]],
                     expected_close: Decimal) -> list[tuple[str, Decimal]]:
    if len({name for name, _ in steps}) != len(steps):
        raise ValueError("step names must be unique")
    running = opening
    levels = [("opening", running)]
    for name, change in steps:
        running += change
        levels.append((name, running))
    if running != expected_close:
        raise ValueError("bridge does not reconcile")
    return levels

bridge = reconcile_bridge(
    Decimal("810.00"),
    [("new contracts", Decimal("147.00")),
     ("returns", Decimal("-59.00")),
     ("credits", Decimal("-81.00"))],
    Decimal("817.00"))
assert bridge[-1] == ("credits", Decimal("817.00"))

Performance and operating cost

For S changes, reconciliation is O(S) time and O(S) output space. The currency example uses Decimal so binary floating-point rounding does not create a false residual. The code validates the exact closing balance but does not check whether step categories overlap or whether source ledger rows were omitted; those are upstream accounting controls. A large waterfall often needs grouped minor steps, with an auditable rollup behind the group.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding a subtotal as though it were another contribution.
  • Forcing the final bar to the reported close despite a residual.
  • Mixing time periods or grains in one bridge.
  • Using color alone to identify increase and decrease.

Validation drill

Explain a move from 810 to 817 units with three signed steps. Then remove the credit step and verify reconciliation fails. Add a subtotal after returns without changing the closing amount.

title: Bullet charts: show a measure, target and performance bands honestly
summary: Keep KPI units and band thresholds explicit instead of compressing context into a gauge.
body:
Keep KPI units and band thresholds explicit instead of compressing context into a gauge.

One axis carries one measure

A bullet chart places an observed value and a target on a shared quantitative scale, often with qualitative background bands. It fits a compact dashboard, but the target and bands must use the same unit and period as the observation. A monthly result against an annual target is not meaningful unless the annual target is allocated by a stated rule. Baseline and axis integrity matter even in a small card. Show the observed number and target in text so the graphic is not the sole carrier of the result.

Treat bands as policy, not decoration

Labels such as below, meets and exceeds imply thresholds selected for a reason. Store the numeric band boundaries and their version. If leadership changes a target, historical cards should either retain the old policy or clearly restate history under the new one. A band extending from 47 to 81 is not an uncertainty interval; it is a classification rule. Uncertainty intervals have a different meaning and should not share the same visual treatment.

Direction changes the interpretation

For revenue, higher may be preferable; for response time, lower may be preferable. The chart's target marker is descriptive until the preferred direction is declared. Put that direction in the accompanying text and label the bands accordingly. A single color progression cannot safely carry this distinction. Accessible text and non-color cues should state whether 68 seconds is better or worse than a target of 59 seconds. A zero target needs a deliberate percentage policy; percent-of-target is undefined there.

Compare cards using a shared contract

Several bullet charts can support comparison only if they use compatible axes or clearly named units. Autoscaling each card to its own maximum makes equal lengths represent different values. If metrics use incompatible units, separate panels and display target-relative gaps explicitly, rather than placing them on one fake common scale. Signed gap views may be clearer for ranking departures from target. Export raw value, target, bands, direction and period. Check missing observations and partial periods before applying a performance label.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def classify_kpi(observed: float, target: float,
                 minimum: float, maximum: float,
                 lower_is_better: bool) -> tuple[float, str]:
    values = (observed, target, minimum, maximum)
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in values):
        raise ValueError("KPI values must be finite")
    if not minimum <= observed <= maximum or not minimum <= target <= maximum:
        raise ValueError("measure or target outside axis")
    gap = observed - target
    meets = observed <= target if lower_is_better else observed >= target
    return gap, "meets target" if meets else "misses target"

response_kpi = classify_kpi(68, 59, 0, 120, lower_is_better=True)
assert response_kpi == (9, "misses target")
revenue_kpi = classify_kpi(81, 59, 0, 120, lower_is_better=False)
assert revenue_kpi == (22, "meets target")

Performance and operating cost

Classifying one card takes O(1) time and space; N cards take O(N). Rendering cost is small, but target lookup and policy versioning dominate operational correctness. The code checks a shared axis and preferred direction. It does not invent background bands or calculate a percentage when the target is zero. Store band thresholds and time period with the emitted card to make historical comparisons reproducible.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing a monthly observed value with an annual target.
  • Using attractive background bands without a stated threshold policy.
  • Assuming higher is always better.
  • Letting each card auto-scale while comparing bar lengths across cards.

Validation drill

Build three service KPI cards: response time, resolved tickets and refund rate. Declare direction, target, axis and band policy for each, then test a missing observation and a zero target.

title: Dual-axis charts: test whether two series really need one plot
summary: Independent vertical scales can manufacture alignment; compare shared-time alternatives first.
body:
Independent vertical scales can manufacture alignment; compare shared-time alternatives first.

Two axes create a choice

A dual-axis chart places two measures against a shared horizontal dimension while giving each its own vertical scale. It can be compact, but independent scale ranges allow almost any pair of trends to look aligned or opposed. State both units, put each series next to its axis label, and inspect the same data as separate aligned panels before publishing. Small multiples preserve time alignment without implying that pixel height has a shared meaning.

Audit the apparent correlation

The eye can mistake coincident peaks for a relationship when one series has been shifted, smoothed or clipped. If the question is whether the measures co-vary, use paired observations in a scatter plot and name any lag rather than inferring it from two lines. Correlation coverage matters when dates are missing from one source. Do not quietly forward-fill one series to align timestamps. Carry measurement cadence and missingness into the displayed record.

When shared axes are possible

If the two series have the same unit and meaning, use a single axis. If they differ only by a constant conversion, convert one before plotting and disclose the conversion. If they have unrelated units but the question is relative change from a baseline, an indexed chart can be clearer, provided the base period and undefined zero-base cases are stated. Transformed scales also demand explicit zero handling. A second axis is not a shortcut around incompatible denominators.

Keep exports and text independent

When a second axis is justified by a particular reading task, export both raw series, scale domains, ticks and units. Use distinct line patterns, not just colors, and name the axes in a text summary. Test the chart with one series removed; readers should still know which axis belongs to the remaining series. The chart manifest should record every transformation and scale domain. Check mobile width: overlapping axis labels can erase the distinctions that made the chart defensible.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def paired_series_rows(
    first: dict[str, float], second: dict[str, float]
) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, float, float]], list[str]]:
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in [*first.values(), *second.values()]):
        raise ValueError("series values must be finite")
    shared = sorted(first.keys() & second.keys())
    missing = sorted(first.keys() ^ second.keys())
    return [(period, first[period], second[period]) for period in shared], missing

requests = {"week-47": 81, "week-48": 97, "week-49": 113}
latency = {"week-47": 59, "week-49": 68, "week-50": 83}
pairs, unpaired = paired_series_rows(requests, latency)
assert pairs == [("week-47", 81, 59), ("week-49", 113, 68)]
assert unpaired == ["week-48", "week-50"]

Performance and operating cost

For A and B keyed observations, set intersection and sorting use O(A+B+K log K) time and O(A+B) additional space for K paired periods. This preparation does not select axis domains or establish a correlation. It prevents silent alignment by index position. A production chart should also validate time-zone and aggregation-period equivalence before treating two keys as the same time.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing independent axis domains solely to align peaks.
  • Forward-filling missing dates without a stated imputation rule.
  • Using two axes for measures that share a convertible unit.
  • Relying on color alone to tie each line to its axis.

Validation drill

Plot weekly requests and latency for 47 weeks as separate aligned panels and as a dual-axis view. Remove two latency weeks and verify the paired observation count changes visibly.

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
summary: Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.
body:
Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.

Area color is not an event count

A choropleth fills geographic regions according to a measure. Large polygons occupy more pixels and can dominate attention even when they contain few people or events. Raw incident counts often track exposure, such as population or active deliveries, more than risk. For a comparable rate, carry numerator and denominator for each polygon and specify the period. Exposure-based rates explain why 8 incidents across 47,000 trips differ from 8 across 470 trips. A map can still show counts when workload is the question; label it as a count map.

Join by stable region identity

Names drift, abbreviations collide, and administrative boundaries change. Join facts to geometry with stable region IDs and a boundary version. Report unmatched fact IDs, polygons with no measure, duplicate assignments and overlapping boundaries before rendering. Spatial joins are a separate operation from coloring polygons; they can duplicate a record if geometries overlap. If one region splits midyear, a before-after map needs a common boundary basis or an explicit break. Do not let a chart library silently drop unmatched regions.

Projection and extent shape perception

A projection transforms coordinates into map space. It can distort area, shape or distance; no flat map preserves everything. For regional comparison, keep the same projection, extent and viewport across panels, and avoid interpreting the visible area of a polygon as its population. Insets for distant regions need clear labels and scale context. If exact comparison of rates matters more than location, provide a sorted bar chart alongside the map. Choose the visual that serves the question, not merely the available geometry.

Class breaks are an editorial decision

Equal-width bins, quantile bins and fixed policy thresholds answer different questions. A quantile palette can assign different colors to tiny numeric differences when many regions cluster tightly; fixed thresholds can leave some colors unused. Print numeric breakpoints and keep them stable when comparing dates. Use a separate treatment for missing data and low-exposure suppression. Color-domain rules carry over to map legends. Keep the original rate in the accessible table and tooltip; color bins are a summary, not the data.

Protect sensitive locations

Very small denominators can make rates unstable and expose information about a few people or facilities. Define a minimum publishable group size, aggregate or suppress as appropriate, and show a visible suppressed state. Do not infer that a blank region has zero risk. Location privacy and small-sample display belong to the same release review. Test a region with no geometry, a polygon with no observation, a zero numerator and a zero denominator separately.

Worked contract

def regional_rates(
    boundary_ids: set[str],
    incident_counts: dict[str, tuple[int, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[str, float | None]]:
    unknown = set(incident_counts) - boundary_ids
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"facts without geometry: {sorted(unknown)}")
    result = {}
    for region_id in boundary_ids:
        if region_id not in incident_counts:
            result[region_id] = ("missing", None)
            continue
        incidents, trips = incident_counts[region_id]
        if not 0 <= incidents <= trips:
            raise ValueError("invalid regional counts")
        result[region_id] = ("no-exposure", None) if trips == 0 else (
            "observed", incidents / trips)
    return result

rates = regional_rates({"zone-47", "zone-81", "zone-94"},
                       {"zone-47": (8, 470), "zone-81": (0, 81)})
assert rates["zone-47"][1] == 8 / 470
assert rates["zone-81"] == ("observed", 0.0)
assert rates["zone-94"] == ("missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For B boundary IDs and M measured regions, this join-and-rate check takes O(B + M) expected time and O(B) output space using hash sets. Rendering cost depends on polygon vertex count, projection and viewport clipping, none of which this code performs. Simplify geometry only to a documented tolerance and keep an exact source for hit tests. A cached tile or geometry file must carry the same boundary version as the measures. The code distinguishes zero and missing; a real publication layer also enforces suppression and uncertainty policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring raw counts as if the map showed per-person or per-trip risk.
  • Joining on human-readable region names without checking unmatched and duplicated keys.
  • Treating a missing polygon or missing measure as zero.
  • Changing map bounds or class breaks between comparison dates.

Validation drill

Map 23 service zones with one split boundary, one missing measure and one zone below the publishable exposure threshold. Reconcile region IDs and rates before drawing polygons; add a sorted rate table for exact comparison.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
summary: Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.
body:
Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.

Use a meaningful baseline

Bar length is read against its baseline. Starting a bar axis at 0.71 can make two completion rates of 0.74 and 0.77 look several times apart. Use zero for ordinary bar lengths and show exact values when a small difference matters. A line chart may use a narrower range to show variation, but the displayed bounds and units must remain obvious.

Inspect transformations

A logarithmic axis can reveal values across orders of magnitude, but equal screen distances then represent equal ratios rather than equal differences. Zero and negative values need an explicit treatment. Never switch an axis to logarithmic merely to fit an outlier, and never compare a linear-panel slope with a log-panel slope as though they share meaning.

Keep category order honest

Sort categories by a documented metric or a stable domain order. If the order changes at each refresh, motion can look like a performance shift when values are steady. Labels should state percent versus percentage points; moving from 74 to 77 percent is a three-point change, not a three-percent relative change. The chart question decides which comparison is primary.

Test presentation rules

Prepare two rates, 0.74 and 0.77, and verify both bars share zero. Then format them as 74.0% and 77.0%. If a narrow view clips labels, retain an accessible text table. Recheck after filtering because an automatic axis may silently rescale and change the apparent difference.

Implementation

def percentage_point_change(previous_rate, current_rate):
    if not all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (previous_rate, current_rate)):
        raise ValueError("rates must be between zero and one")
    return (current_rate - previous_rate) * 100

change_points = percentage_point_change(0.74, 0.77)

Performance and operating cost

Scale formatting is O(M) for M plotted marks. The larger cost is review: test every filter state that changes axis bounds, zero visibility or label collisions. Cache formatted labels only when underlying rate and unit versions match.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not truncate a bar axis without making the baseline explicit.
  • Do not label a percentage-point movement as a relative percent.
  • Do not hide nonpositive observations when using a logarithmic scale.

title: Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together
summary: Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.
body:
Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.

An image is not the full evidence

A PNG captures pixels; it does not preserve the records, filter predicates, missingness states or exact values behind them. SVG retains scalable geometry, but it can still omit the underlying analytical contract. For a decision-grade chart, export an image, a machine-readable table of plotted values and a manifest describing the query and rendering choices. The package should answer which source snapshot, cohort, units, time zone, grouping rule, axis domain, palette and code version produced the picture. Dashboard provenance supplies these ingredients; export binds them to an artifact.

Version the plotted data product

A chart may use raw events, daily aggregates or a reduced display level. The export must name that level. Include a dataset snapshot or immutable revision, plus the report's as-of time when corrections are possible. A hash of canonical manifest bytes detects accidental changes to the manifest; it does not authenticate a source by itself. If integrity across systems matters, sign the package through a trusted release path. Never include private identifiers or unmasked rows merely because a chart view was authorized. Data classification still governs exports.

Keep visible and downloadable values aligned

The CSV or JSON table must use the same filters, denominator, sort, unit and missing-value policy as the displayed chart. If the chart shows rounded percentages, include underlying counts and unrounded rates in the data export while documenting the display rounding. A tooltip, table and image title should agree on the period and finalization status. Linked filters can change the cohort moments before a user clicks export; capture one state and one data version atomically for the whole package.

Make the visual portable and accessible

An SVG is useful for vector editing and high-resolution print, but font substitution and external styles can change its appearance. A PNG is more predictable but loses scale and selectable text. Include an accessible text summary and data table in either case. Document the output size, color profile where relevant, and the scale tick labels. Text alternatives should describe the main pattern, notable exceptions and uncertainty rather than repeat a generic chart title. For a public download, test that no hidden private series remain in SVG markup or embedded metadata.

Recreate before release

Re-run the export from its manifest in a clean environment. Compare plotted counts, axis limits, filters, title, source generation and checksum, allowing only declared rendering differences such as font rasterization. A changed query definition should make an old package non-reproducible by design; report that conflict instead of silently rendering with today's code. Keep an editorial preview for review, then publish an immutable artifact reference when the chart is used in a report or audit. Reduced series need the level and bucket rule in the manifest.

Worked contract

import hashlib
import json

def chart_manifest(query_id: str, dataset_version: str,
                   filters: dict[str, list[str]],
                   axis_domain: tuple[float, float],
                   plotted_rows: int) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    if not query_id or not dataset_version or plotted_rows < 0:
        raise ValueError("missing chart identity")
    if axis_domain[0] >= axis_domain[1]:
        raise ValueError("invalid axis domain")
    manifest = {
        "query_id": query_id,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "filters": {key: sorted(set(values))
                    for key, values in sorted(filters.items())},
        "y_axis_domain": list(axis_domain),
        "plotted_rows": plotted_rows,
        "unit": "minutes",
        "render_contract": "depot-delay-v3",
    }
    payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                         ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
    return manifest, hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

first = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                       {"region": ["north", "north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
second = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                        {"region": ["north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
assert first == second and len(first[1]) == 64

Performance and operating cost

For F total filter values and M serialized manifest bytes, sorting normalized filters costs O(F log F) in the worst case; JSON encoding and SHA-256 hashing take O(M) time and O(M) temporary memory. Exporting an image or plotted data can cost much more and depends on the renderer and row count. This hash identifies equal manifest bytes, not equal pixels or trustworthy provenance. Add a data-file checksum and a signed release record when the export package crosses a trust boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Publishing only a screenshot when reviewers need the plotted data and cohort definition.
  • Exporting a CSV from a stale filter state while the chart shows a newer selection.
  • Assuming a manifest hash proves who created the data.
  • Embedding hidden private rows in an otherwise public SVG or HTML export.

Validation drill

Export one filtered depot-delay chart as SVG and CSV with a manifest. Change only the filter and verify the manifest digest changes, then rebuild the original chart from its saved version and compare counts and axis bounds.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.
